You get access to the same EC2 instance types, EBS storage, and even managed services like Amazon RDS and Amazon ECS that you'd use in the cloud, but running locally on infrastructure you can physically touch.

The architectural driver for Outposts is ultra-low latency between your AWS workloads and on-premises systems or data that cannot be moved to the cloud. Consider a manufacturing plant with industrial control systems that generate massive amounts of sensor data requiring real-time processing, or a hospital with medical imaging equipment that produces large files needing immediate analysis by machine learning models. In both cases, moving the data to the cloud for processing introduces latency that's unacceptable. But running the compute locally without AWS's managed services means giving up the operational benefits, scalability, and breadth of services that make the cloud attractive. Outposts solves this dilemma by bringing AWS to where your data is.

Outposts comes in two form factors. The **Outposts rack** is a 42U rack (or multiple racks for larger deployments) that AWS delivers, installs, and maintains in your data center. It provides substantial compute and storage capacity – enough to run significant workloads locally. The **Outposts server**, a smaller 1U or 2U form factor, is designed for locations with limited space or power, such as retail stores, branch offices, or factory floors with space constraints. Both form factors provide the same fundamental capability: a piece of AWS infrastructure that runs in your facility, managed by AWS, and connected back to a parent AWS Region.

The services available on Outposts are a subset of what's available in AWS Regions, but it's a meaningful subset designed to support common workloads. For **compute**, you can run Amazon EC2 instances using standard instance types and Amazon Machine Images. For **storage**, you have Amazon EBS volumes for block storage and Amazon S3 on Outposts for object storage. For **containers**, you can deploy workloads on Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS, allowing you to run Kubernetes or ECS-orchestrated containerized applications locally. For **databases**, Amazon RDS on Outposts provides managed relational databases running on the local infrastructure. For **networking**, you configure Amazon VPC on Outposts, creating subnets that are logical extensions of your VPC in the parent Region, and you use Application Load Balancers to distribute traffic to your local applications.

The networking architecture is particularly important for understanding Outposts. When you deploy an Outposts rack, you create a **local gateway** that acts as the default route for traffic between your Outposts VPC subnets and your on-premises network. This local gateway enables single-digit millisecond latency between applications running on Outposts and your on-premises systems or data sources – this is the core value proposition. Meanwhile, Outposts requires a **service link** – a reliable, high-bandwidth network connection back to the parent AWS Region. This service link is used for management traffic, for accessing AWS services not available locally (like AWS IAM for authentication, Amazon CloudWatch for monitoring, and AWS Systems Manager for operational tasks), and for data synchronization. Critically, the service link is not in the data path for latency-sensitive workloads; those stay local via the local gateway.

This architecture creates several important characteristics. First, your latency-sensitive application components run on Outposts, achieving single-digit millisecond latency to on-premises systems, while less latency-sensitive components – like your databases' long-term backup storage or your centralized logging and monitoring – can remain in the AWS Region. Second, you manage your Outposts infrastructure using the same AWS Management Console, CLI, and APIs you use for Region-based resources. An Outposts subnet appears in your VPC just like any other subnet; you launch EC2 instances the same way; you use the same IAM roles and policies. This operational consistency is a major benefit. Third, AWS handles the physical maintenance, hardware replacement, and infrastructure lifecycle management for the Outposts hardware, dramatically reducing operational burden compared to managing equivalent on-premises infrastructure yourself.

Common use cases for Outposts in hybrid architectures include **manufacturing execution systems (MES)** that require real-time control of factory equipment with latency measured in milliseconds, **healthcare applications** where medical devices produce data that must be processed locally for regulatory or latency reasons, **financial services** applications like algorithmic trading systems or ATM fleets requiring local processing, **media and entertainment** workflows where massive video files must be processed at production facilities, and **telecommunications** applications at the network edge requiring local compute for 5G or other latency-sensitive services.

#### AWS Local Zones: Metro-Area Extensions for End-User Latency

While AWS Outposts addresses latency between AWS infrastructure and your on-premises systems, AWS Local Zones address a different problem: latency between end-users in specific metropolitan areas and the nearest AWS Region. Standard AWS Regions are located in major geographic areas, but they're not in every city. A user in Boston connecting to an application running in the US East (N. Virginia) Region, roughly 400 miles away, experiences baseline latency due to that distance. For most applications, this is acceptable. But for workloads requiring single-digit millisecond latency to end-users – like real-time gaming, live video streaming, or augmented reality applications – this distance-based latency is problematic.

AWS Local Zones are extensions of AWS Regions deployed in metropolitan areas to bring compute, storage, and database services closer to end-users. Each Local Zone is connected back to a parent Region via redundant, high-bandwidth private network connections, but it's physically located much closer to populations of users in specific cities. When you use a Local Zone, you're essentially extending your VPC from the parent Region into that metro area, creating subnets within the Local Zone where you can launch resources.

The architectural pattern is to run your latency-sensitive application components – the frontend web servers, real-time API endpoints, or game servers – in the Local Zone, while keeping less latency-sensitive components like databases, long-term storage, or analytics workloads in the parent Region. This hybrid architecture gives you the performance of local compute while maintaining the full breadth of AWS services in the Region.

Consider a real-time multiplayer gaming scenario. The game client on a user's device in Los Angeles needs to send player actions to the game server and receive world state updates with minimal latency. Deploying the game servers in the Los Angeles Local Zone, rather than in a Region potentially hundreds of miles away, reduces round-trip latency to single-digit milliseconds. Meanwhile, the game's central database, which stores player accounts and game state but can tolerate somewhat higher latency, runs in the parent US West (Oregon) Region. The game servers in the Local Zone communicate with this central database over the high-bandwidth connection between the Local Zone and the Region. Players get responsive gameplay, while the architecture benefits from the Region's full suite of services for the backend.

Other common use cases include **media and entertainment production**, where editing workstations in a city need low-latency access to compute and storage for 4K/8K video rendering; **augmented reality (AR) applications for e-commerce**, where mobile users need real-time 3D model rendering; **financial services applications** serving customers in specific metro areas with latency-sensitive trading or transaction processing; and **healthcare applications** where real-time telemedicine or medical image processing must happen close to hospitals in particular cities.

The key architectural distinction between Local Zones and Outposts is the target: Local Zones optimize latency to end-users in a metro area, while Outposts optimize latency to on-premises systems in your data center. Local Zones are AWS-operated infrastructure in AWS-controlled facilities; you don't have physical access to the hardware. Outposts are AWS-operated infrastructure installed in your facility, where you control physical access. Both are managed by AWS, both extend a parent Region, but they solve different latency problems.

#### Snowball Edge Compute Optimized: Disconnected Edge Computing

AWS Snowball Edge represents a fundamentally different architectural approach. While Outposts and Local Zones maintain constant connectivity to a parent AWS Region – they're *extensions* of the cloud – Snowball Edge Compute Optimized is designed for environments that are disconnected from the cloud entirely or have only intermittent connectivity. This is edge computing in its purest form: compute capacity that operates autonomously, often in harsh or remote environments, collecting and processing data locally, and periodically syncing results back to AWS when connectivity is available.

The physical device is a ruggedized, portable appliance designed to withstand challenging conditions. It's been used on ships at sea, in remote mining operations, on military deployments, in disaster recovery scenarios, and on factory floors where internet connectivity is unreliable. The compute capability is substantial – Snowball Edge Compute Optimized provides 52 vCPUs, 208 GB of memory, and optional GPU acceleration, along with 42 TB of usable block storage. This is enough capacity to run meaningful workloads locally.

The architectural pattern shifts from the connected models of Outposts and Local Zones to a **local-first** design. Your application runs entirely on the Snowball Edge device, processing data generated by local sensors, cameras, industrial equipment, or other sources without needing to communicate with AWS. The device runs a subset of AWS services locally – EC2 instances for compute, S3-compatible object storage for data, Lambda functions for event-driven processing – all operating independently of the cloud. When network connectivity becomes available, whether through satellite uplink, periodic connection to a network, or physical transport of the device back to a facility with internet access, data collected and processed on the device can be transferred to AWS for long-term storage, further analysis, or integration with cloud-based systems.

Common use cases highlight the disconnected nature: **industrial IoT in remote locations** like oil rigs, mines, or offshore wind farms, where sensors generate data that must be processed locally due to lack of reliable connectivity; **military and tactical operations** requiring compute at the edge of the network in environments where connectivity to cloud regions is unavailable or insecure; **maritime operations** on ships where satellite connectivity is expensive and intermittent, but local processing of navigation, monitoring, or cargo data is critical; **disaster recovery and emergency response**, where Snowball Edge devices can be rapidly deployed to provide compute capacity in areas where infrastructure has been damaged; and **connected vehicles and autonomous systems** where processing must happen locally due to latency requirements and connectivity constraints.

Snowball Edge devices can be clustered together to increase both compute capacity and storage, providing **resiliency** through redundancy. In a clustered configuration, if one device fails, the others continue operating, and data is replicated across devices for durability. This clustering capability makes Snowball Edge suitable for more permanent edge installations where increased capacity and fault tolerance are needed, not just temporary or mobile deployments.

#### Comparing the Three: Choosing the Right Solution

The architectural decision between Outposts, Local Zones, and Snowball Edge comes down to answering three key questions: What are you trying to minimize latency to? What level of connectivity to AWS do you have? What operational model do you need?

**AWS Outposts** is the right choice when your primary need is low latency to on-premises systems or data, you have reliable network connectivity to an AWS Region, you want AWS managed services running in your facility, and you need substantial, sustained compute capacity locally. The operational model is fully managed by AWS, and it's designed for permanent installations in data centers or large facilities.

**AWS Local Zones** are appropriate when you need to minimize latency to end-users in a specific metropolitan area, those users are connecting from fixed networks (broadband, not mobile 5G), your application can tolerate the limited service subset available in Local Zones, and you want a fully cloud-operational model without managing physical infrastructure. Local Zones are AWS-operated and accessed identically to Region resources.

**Snowball Edge Compute Optimized** is the solution when you have disconnected or highly intermittent connectivity, need local compute in remote or harsh environments, require portability or rapid deployment, can design your application to operate autonomously for extended periods, and need the ruggedization and form factor of a portable appliance. The operational model requires more direct device management, and it's designed for temporary deployments or permanent edge installations where connectivity to AWS is not reliable.

For the SAA exam, recognizing the architectural drivers for each service is key. A scenario describing single-digit millisecond latency to on-premises industrial equipment with a reliable connection to AWS points to Outposts. A scenario about reducing latency for gamers in a specific city points to Local Zones. A scenario involving remote operations with no reliable internet connectivity points to Snowball Edge. Understanding these distinctions demonstrates your grasp of how AWS addresses the full spectrum of latency requirements in hybrid and edge computing architectures.

## 3.9.5 Scaling Across Boundaries: Managing Growth During and After Migration

As an organization grows, the hybrid network must be able to scale to accommodate more traffic and connections. The migration process itself must be scalable to handle large volumes of data and servers. A primary goal of migration is often to move applications from a fixed-capacity, on-premises environment to a scalable, elastic architecture in the cloud.

The scalability challenges in a migration and hybrid cloud context are fundamentally different from those in a purely cloud-native environment. Here, we're not simply designing for growth — we're bridging two worlds with different scaling paradigms. On-premises infrastructure typically scales vertically and in discrete, capital-intensive increments. You buy a bigger server, or you add another blade to the chassis, and that capacity sits there whether you're using it or not. Cloud infrastructure, by contrast, was built from the ground up for horizontal scaling and elasticity, allowing resources to grow and shrink dynamically based on demand. The challenge for the architect is twofold: first, to ensure that the bridge between these environments — the network — can scale without becoming a bottleneck; and second, to transform applications during migration so they can take advantage of cloud-native scaling patterns once they land in AWS.

This section explores scalability across four distinct architectural domains. We begin by examining how to scale the hybrid network infrastructure itself, ensuring that connectivity between on-premises and AWS can grow to meet increasing demands without requiring a complete redesign. We then analyze how to achieve cloud-native scalability for applications that have been migrated, contrasting the operational models of traditional on-premises scaling with the elastic, automated patterns available in AWS. Next, we delve into database scaling strategies that span both environments, addressing the unique challenges of maintaining performance and consistency while data resides in two locations during a migration, and exploring post-migration optimization patterns. Finally, we examine the specialized domain of hybrid container workloads, where orchestration platforms like Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS extend their reach into on-premises data centers, enabling a consistent operational model for containerized applications across the entire hybrid landscape.

### Scaling the Hybrid Network Infrastructure

The network connection between your on-premises environment and AWS is more than just a data pipeline — it's the foundation upon which your entire hybrid architecture rests. As your cloud footprint grows, as more applications migrate, and as traffic between environments increases, this connection must scale to meet demand. Unlike a traditional data center network where you might simply add more switches to a stack or increase port density, scaling hybrid connectivity requires careful architectural planning. The decisions you make here will determine whether your network becomes an enabler of growth or a constraining bottleneck that forces you to rethink your entire migration strategy.

The scalability challenge manifests in two primary dimensions: bandwidth and topology. Bandwidth is the straightforward part — you need enough throughput to handle the volume of data moving between environments. But topology is where the real architectural complexity emerges. A simple point-to-point connection might work for a pilot migration, but as you add more VPCs in AWS, more on-premises sites, and more complex routing requirements, you quickly outgrow that model. The question becomes: how do you design a network that can grow from connecting a handful of resources to potentially hundreds of VPCs and multiple data centers, all while maintaining security, manageability, and cost-effectiveness?

The evolution of hybrid network scaling on AWS mirrors a broader shift in network architecture thinking. Early AWS adopters often started with a single VPN connection or a single Direct Connect link, connecting one VPC to one on-premises location. As their needs grew, they added more connections, creating a mesh of VPN tunnels or multiple Direct Connect circuits. This worked, but it didn't scale. Each new connection required manual configuration, routing became increasingly complex, and operational overhead grew exponentially. The introduction of AWS Transit Gateway fundamentally changed this paradigm, offering a hub-and-spoke model that could scale to thousands of connections while maintaining centralized management and consistent policies. Understanding when and how to leverage this service, versus continuing with simpler connection models, is a critical skill for the solutions architect designing for growth.

#### The Limits of VPN Mesh Architectures

Let's begin by understanding what *doesn't* scale, because it illuminates why the more sophisticated patterns exist. When you create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between your on-premises network and a VPC, you're establishing a direct, point-to-point encrypted tunnel. This works beautifully for a single VPC. But imagine you now have five VPCs, each representing a different application environment, and all of them need to communicate with your on-premises data center. The naive approach is to create a separate VPN connection from your on-premises Customer Gateway to each VPC. You now have five independent tunnels to manage, five sets of routing configurations to maintain, and five points where a misconfiguration could break connectivity.

Now add a second on-premises site — perhaps a disaster recovery data center or a remote office that also needs to access AWS resources. If you want each on-premises site to connect to each VPC independently, you're quickly building a mesh network with exponentially growing complexity. With just two on-premises sites and five VPCs, you're managing ten VPN connections. Scale that to ten on-premises sites and twenty VPCs, and you're looking at two hundred individual VPN connections, each with its own configuration, routing table, and operational overhead. This is not just a management nightmare; it's a scaling anti-pattern.

Beyond the operational burden, there's a performance ceiling. Each Site-to-Site VPN connection is typically limited by the throughput capacity of the Customer Gateway appliance on your on-premises side. While AWS supports Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing to aggregate bandwidth across multiple VPN tunnels, you're still constrained by the processing power of your on-premises hardware, which must encrypt and decrypt every packet. For high-bandwidth workloads or latency-sensitive applications, a mesh of VPN connections simply cannot scale to meet enterprise demands. This is where the hub-and-spoke model, enabled by AWS Transit Gateway, becomes essential.

#### AWS Transit Gateway: The Hub-and-Spoke Solution for Scalable Hybrid Connectivity

AWS Transit Gateway was purpose-built to solve the hybrid network scaling problem. Think of it as a cloud-native router that sits in the middle of your AWS infrastructure, acting as a central hub through which all of your VPCs, VPN connections, and Direct Connect links can communicate. Instead of creating a mesh of point-to-point connections, you attach each VPC and each on-premises connection to the Transit Gateway once. The Transit Gateway then handles all the routing between them, using a single, centralized routing table (or multiple tables for more complex segmentation requirements). This architectural shift — from mesh to hub-and-spoke — is what enables true scalability.

Let's make this concrete. Imagine you have ten VPCs in your AWS environment, representing different application tiers, business units, or environments (development, staging, production). Without Transit Gateway, connecting these VPCs to each other would require VPC peering connections — a potential 45 individual peering relationships for full mesh connectivity among just ten VPCs. Now add your on-premises data center into the mix. Each VPC that needs on-premises access would require its own VPN or Direct Connect attachment, multiplying your configuration overhead. With Transit Gateway, you attach each of those ten VPCs to the Transit Gateway once. You attach your on-premises connection (whether VPN or Direct Connect) to the Transit Gateway once. The Transit Gateway's routing table controls which VPCs can talk to each other and which can reach on-premises, all managed from a single control plane.

The scalability numbers are significant. A single Transit Gateway can support up to 5,000 VPC attachments and an aggregate bandwidth of up to 50 Gbps per Availability Zone for VPN connections using ECMP. For Direct Connect, you can attach multiple Direct Connect Gateways to a Transit Gateway, effectively allowing you to scale your hybrid bandwidth to hundreds of gigabits per second if needed. Equally important, the operational complexity remains constant. Adding your twentieth VPC is no more difficult than adding your second VPC — you simply create a new attachment and update the Transit Gateway route table. This "constant complexity" model is the hallmark of a scalable architecture.

Beyond the raw connection capacity, Transit Gateway enables advanced routing and segmentation strategies that are critical for enterprise-scale hybrid environments. You can create multiple route tables within a single Transit Gateway, each with different routing policies, and associate different VPC attachments with different route tables. This allows you to implement network segmentation at scale — for example, isolating development VPCs from production VPCs, while allowing both to reach on-premises via the same physical connection but with different firewall rules applied. You can also use Transit Gateway Network Manager to gain centralized visibility and monitoring across your entire global network, including both AWS and on-premises components. This level of operational insight is simply not possible with a decentralized mesh architecture.

  <figcaption style="text-align: center; font-style: italic; margin-top: 10px;">Transit Gateway uses multiple route tables to achieve network segmentation. Development and production VPCs attach to different route tables within the same Transit Gateway, allowing both environments to reach on-premises while remaining isolated from each other.</figcaption>

#### Scaling AWS Direct Connect Bandwidth

While Transit Gateway solves the topology and connection count problem, you still need sufficient bandwidth on the underlying physical connections to handle your traffic volumes. For many organizations, especially those migrating large workloads or maintaining latency-sensitive hybrid applications, AWS Direct Connect is the preferred connectivity method due to its consistent performance and higher bandwidth options compared to internet-based VPNs. Scaling Direct Connect bandwidth is a different challenge than scaling VPN, because you're dealing with physical circuits and dedicated network ports, not just software-defined tunnels.

The most straightforward way to scale a Direct Connect connection is to upgrade the port speed. Direct Connect offers port speeds of 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps, and 100 Gbps. If your workload has outgrown a 1 Gbps connection, you can request an upgrade to a 10 Gbps connection, assuming your on-premises network infrastructure can support it. This is vertical scaling — you're making the pipe bigger. However, this approach has practical limits. Upgrading a port often requires coordination with your network provider, may involve downtime during the cutover, and eventually you hit the ceiling of what's available (100 Gbps is the current maximum for a single Direct Connect port).

For greater bandwidth and resilience, you can implement horizontal scaling by creating multiple Direct Connect connections and aggregating them using Link Aggregation Groups (LAGs). A LAG allows you to bundle multiple physical connections — up to four 100 Gbps connections, for a theoretical maximum of 400 Gbps — and treat them as a single, logical connection from a routing perspective. AWS uses Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP) to manage the LAG, distributing traffic across the member connections using a hash-based algorithm. This provides not only increased bandwidth but also redundancy: if one physical connection fails, traffic automatically flows over the remaining connections in the LAG without requiring any routing changes.

There's a critical architectural consideration here: LAG connections must terminate at the same Direct Connect location. This means that while a LAG provides redundancy against individual connection failures, it does not protect against a failure of the entire Direct Connect facility. For true high availability, you need to establish Direct Connect connections to multiple geographically diverse Direct Connect locations and rely on dynamic routing (BGP) to fail over between them. We discussed this availability pattern in more detail in section 3.9.3, but it's important to note here that scaling bandwidth and scaling for resilience are related but distinct concerns. An architect must design for both.

#### Integrating Direct Connect with Transit Gateway for Enterprise Scale

To understand how Direct Connect scales in a hybrid environment, you need to grasp the complete connection topology, because each layer serves a specific architectural purpose. The full path from your on-premises network to your AWS VPCs follows this chain: **On-Premises Router → Direct Connect (potentially in a LAG) → Direct Connect Gateway (DXGW) → Transit Gateway (TGW) → VPCs**.

Let's break down why each component is necessary and how they work together to enable scale.

Your **on-premises router** is the starting point, establishing a BGP session that advertises your internal network prefixes to AWS. This router connects to one or more **Direct Connect circuits** (which may be bundled into a LAG for bandwidth aggregation). The Direct Connect connection terminates at a Direct Connect location, where AWS's networking equipment sits. But here's the critical point: a Direct Connect connection by itself doesn't know *where* in AWS to send your traffic. It's just a physical pipe. As we introduced in 3.3.3, you need to attach a **Virtual Interface (VIF)** to give it a destination.

For connecting to Transit Gateway, you create a **Transit Virtual Interface (Transit VIF)**, which is associated with a **Direct Connect Gateway (DXGW)**. This is where many architects get confused, so let's be explicit: the Direct Connect Gateway is not optional in this topology. You cannot connect a Direct Connect circuit directly to a Transit Gateway. The DXGW acts as an intermediary routing layer that bridges the physical Direct Connect world with the logical Transit Gateway world.

::: {.callout-box data-type="sidebar"}

### The Legacy Direct Connect Architecture — Before Transit Gateway

Before Transit Gateway became available in 2018, connecting multiple VPCs to on-premises networks through Direct Connect required a different architecture that quickly hit scalability limits. Understanding this legacy pattern helps clarify why Transit Gateway represents such a significant architectural improvement and why you may still encounter this pattern on the exam or in existing AWS environments.

In the pre-Transit Gateway era, the path from on-premises to AWS VPCs followed this topology: **On-Premises Router → Direct Connect → Direct Connect Gateway → Virtual Private Gateways (VGWs) → VPCs**. Each VPC that needed on-premises connectivity required its own Virtual Private Gateway, which is a regional, VPC-specific resource that terminates VPN and Direct Connect connections. The Direct Connect Gateway could aggregate multiple Direct Connect circuits and route traffic to multiple VPCs, but it connected to those VPCs through individual Virtual Private Gateways, not through a centralized regional hub.

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src="images/dx-dxgw-vgw-legacy.svg" alt="Legacy Direct Connect architecture showing DXGW connecting to individual Virtual Private Gateways, each attached to a separate VPC" />
  <figcaption style="font-style: italic; color: #555;">The legacy Direct Connect architecture: A Direct Connect Gateway connects to individual Virtual Private Gateways (maximum 10), with each VGW attached to a single VPC. VPCs cannot communicate with each other through this topology.</figcaption>
</figure>

The critical limitation was this: **a single Direct Connect Gateway could only be associated with up to 10 Virtual Private Gateways**. This meant that if you had 50 VPCs that needed on-premises access, you would need at least five separate Direct Connect Gateways, each managing a subset of your VPCs. The operational complexity multiplied quickly. Moreover, VPCs connected through this architecture could not communicate with each other — they could only reach on-premises. If VPC A needed to talk to VPC B, you had to use VPC peering or route traffic back through your on-premises network, both of which introduced additional latency and configuration overhead.

Transit Gateway eliminated these constraints entirely. A single Transit Gateway can support thousands of VPC attachments, and VPCs attached to the same Transit Gateway can communicate with each other directly over the AWS backbone without hairpinning through on-premises. The Direct Connect Gateway still exists in the architecture, but now it connects to Transit Gateways rather than individual Virtual Private Gateways, allowing the same DXGW to provide on-premises connectivity to hundreds or thousands of VPCs across multiple regions. This is why the Transit Gateway model is considered the modern, scalable approach for enterprise hybrid networking — it breaks through the hard limits of the VGW-based architecture while simplifying operations dramatically.

:::

Why does AWS require this intermediate layer? The answer lies in the global nature of AWS networking and the need for a stable, region-independent abstraction. A single Direct Connect Gateway can be associated with multiple Transit Gateways in different AWS Regions, allowing your on-premises network to reach VPCs across the globe through a single Direct Connect connection. The DXGW handles the complex task of routing your traffic to the appropriate regional Transit Gateway based on BGP advertisements, while the Transit Gateway then routes to the specific VPCs within that region. This two-tier hub design — DXGW for global routing, TGW for regional routing — is what enables the architecture to scale to thousands of VPCs across multiple regions.

<figure style="text-align: center;">
  <img src="images/dx-dxgw-tgw-topology.svg" alt="Complete Direct Connect to Transit Gateway topology showing the full connection path from on-premises through each gateway layer to VPCs." />
  <figcaption style="font-style: italic; color: #555;">The complete enterprise-scale Direct Connect topology: on-premises routers connect via Direct Connect (potentially aggregated in a LAG) to a Direct Connect Gateway, which routes to Transit Gateways in multiple regions, each providing access to dozens or hundreds of VPCs. Each layer provides independent scalability: physical bandwidth, global routing, and regional VPC aggregation.</figcaption>
</figure>

From a bandwidth perspective, this integration model means you can attach multiple Direct Connect connections (from different locations, potentially in different regions) to the same Direct Connect Gateway, and that DXGW can then feed all of that aggregated bandwidth to a single Transit Gateway. The Transit Gateway supports up to 50 Gbps of bandwidth per VPC attachment, and its total throughput capacity scales with the number of Availability Zones in which it operates. By combining multiple high-bandwidth Direct Connect links with Transit Gateway's massive internal backplane, you can build hybrid networks capable of moving terabytes of data per hour between on-premises and hundreds of VPCs.

Let's make this concrete with an example. Imagine you have a large enterprise with three on-premises data centers in different geographic regions (US East, US West, Europe), and you're operating AWS infrastructure in four AWS Regions (us-east-1, us-west-2, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1) with 50 VPCs per region, for a total of 200 VPCs. You establish a 10 Gbps Direct Connect connection from each on-premises data center to the nearest Direct Connect location — three connections total. You create a single Direct Connect Gateway and attach all three Direct Connect connections to it via Transit VIFs. You then associate this DXGW with four Transit Gateways, one in each AWS Region. Finally, you attach all 50 VPCs in each region to their respective Transit Gateway.

From an operational perspective, you've created three physical connections and configured one Direct Connect Gateway. But from a connectivity perspective, you've just enabled full mesh communication between three on-premises sites and 200 VPCs across four AWS Regions. The routing is handled automatically by BGP: each Transit Gateway advertises the CIDR blocks of its attached VPCs to the DXGW, and the DXGW advertises your on-premises network prefixes to each Transit Gateway. When a server in your US East data center needs to reach a VPC in ap-southeast-1, the traffic flows from your on-premises router, across the Direct Connect link, through the DXGW (which routes it to the Asia-Pacific Transit Gateway), and finally to the target VPC. The entire path is over the AWS global backbone — fast, consistent, and secure.

This architecture also gives you powerful traffic engineering capabilities. Using BGP attributes like AS path prepending, local preference, and community tags, you can implement policies that direct certain types of traffic over specific Direct Connect connections. For example, you might prefer to route traffic destined for us-east-1 VPCs over your US East Direct Connect link, and only fail over to the US West link if the primary path is unavailable. Or you might configure the DXGW to load-balance traffic across all available connections based on a hash of the source and destination IP addresses. These are advanced patterns, but they're essential tools in the architect's toolkit for managing performance and cost at enterprise scale.

The key takeaway is this: when you're designing a hybrid network that needs to scale to hundreds of VPCs and multiple on-premises sites, the combination of Direct Connect, Direct Connect Gateway, and Transit Gateway provides a three-tier architecture that separates concerns cleanly. Direct Connect provides the physical bandwidth. The Direct Connect Gateway provides global routing and multi-region connectivity. Transit Gateway provides regional routing and VPC aggregation. Each layer is independently scalable, and together they enable hybrid architectures of nearly unlimited size and complexity.

#### Choosing the Right Architecture for Your Scale

Not every organization needs the complexity of Transit Gateway or the bandwidth of multiple 100 Gbps Direct Connect links. The key architectural skill is knowing when to adopt these scalable patterns. For a small organization with one or two VPCs and a single on-premises site, a simple Site-to-Site VPN connection to a Virtual Private Gateway is perfectly adequate and far more cost-effective. The complexity and cost of Transit Gateway would be overkill.

The inflection point typically comes when you start managing more than five to ten VPCs that need on-premises connectivity, or when you anticipate rapid growth in your AWS footprint. At that scale, the operational overhead of managing individual VPN connections or VPC peering relationships starts to outweigh the incremental cost of Transit Gateway. Similarly, if your bandwidth requirements are modest — perhaps a few hundred megabits per second of sustained traffic — a VPN connection will likely suffice. But if you're migrating large databases, running real-time replication, or supporting latency-sensitive applications with high throughput needs, Direct Connect becomes not just an optimization but a requirement.

The most scalable hybrid network architectures are designed with growth in mind from the beginning. Even if you start with a single VPC and a single VPN connection, you can architect with the knowledge that you'll eventually migrate to Transit Gateway. This means, for example, ensuring your IP addressing scheme allows for future expansion, and using consistent tagging and naming conventions that will make the eventual migration to a more complex topology operationally manageable. It means documenting your routing policies clearly, so that when you add the tenth VPC, you're not reverse-engineering the intent of configurations that were put in place years earlier. Scalability isn't just about the services you choose; it's about the operational discipline and forethought you bring to the design.

### Achieving Cloud-Native Scalability for Migrated Applications

Once you've established a scalable network to bridge your on-premises environment and AWS, the next challenge is ensuring that the applications themselves can take advantage of cloud-native scaling patterns. This is where the rubber meets the road in migration architecture. You can build the most sophisticated hybrid network imaginable, but if your applications remain locked in the scaling paradigms of the on-premises world, you haven't truly migrated to the cloud. You've simply relocated your infrastructure to someone else's data center.

The fundamental promise of cloud computing is elasticity: the ability to scale resources up and down dynamically in response to demand, paying only for what you use. But elasticity isn't automatic. It's an architectural property that must be designed into your applications, and it's directly influenced by the migration strategy you choose. An application that's been "lifted and shifted" via a Rehost migration retains its original architecture, which often means it's stateful, vertically scaled, and requires manual intervention to add capacity. An application that's been refactored to leverage cloud-native services can scale horizontally and automatically, without human intervention. Understanding this relationship between migration strategy and scalability is critical for the solutions architect.

#### Contrasting On-Premises and Cloud Scaling Models

In a traditional on-premises data center, scalability was constrained by physics and procurement timelines. If your application needed more capacity, you had two options: vertical scaling (upgrading to a more powerful server) or horizontal scaling (adding more servers to the cluster). Vertical scaling was simpler from an application perspective — you just needed more RAM or faster CPUs — but it had hard limits and often required downtime to perform the hardware swap. Horizontal scaling offered greater ultimate capacity, but it required that your application be designed to distribute load across multiple servers, which many legacy applications simply weren't built to do.

Both approaches shared a common characteristic: capacity was provisioned based on peak demand projections, not actual usage. You had to buy enough hardware to handle your busiest day of the year, which meant that most of the time, that hardware sat idle. This was the CapEx model — large upfront investments in fixed assets that depreciated over time. There was no elasticity, only over-provisioning for peak load or accepting degraded performance during demand spikes.

AWS fundamentally changes this equation by offering virtually unlimited capacity that can be provisioned in minutes and billed by the hour (or second, for some services). Horizontal scaling becomes the default pattern, enabled by services like Elastic Load Balancing and EC2 Auto Scaling Groups, which we covered in depth in section 3.1.3.2. These services allow you to define policies that automatically add or remove instances based on real-time metrics like CPU utilization, request count, or custom application metrics. During peak demand, your application scales out; during quiet periods, it scales in, reducing costs. This is the OpEx model — variable costs that align with actual business value delivered.

But here's the critical insight: these scaling patterns require a specific application architecture. They require statelessness. If your application stores user session data on the local disk of a web server, you cannot simply add or remove servers at will, because users would lose their sessions. If your application has hard-coded IP addresses pointing to specific backend servers, you cannot dynamically change the server pool. The migration strategy you choose — Rehost, Replatform, or Refactor — determines how much work is required to achieve true cloud-native scalability.

#### The Impact of Migration Strategy on Scalability

Let's ground this in concrete examples. Suppose you have a three-tier web application running on-premises: a layer of web servers, a layer of application servers, and a relational database. You decide to perform a Rehost migration using AWS Application Migration Service (AWS MGN), which we discussed in section 3.9.0. MGN performs block-level replication of your servers to AWS, creating EC2 instances that are functionally identical to your on-premises machines. This is fast — you can complete the migration in days or weeks — but the resulting architecture is a mirror of what you had before.

Those EC2 instances are still using local disk to store session state. They're still sized based on your on-premises capacity planning, which was probably overly conservative. You can manually add more EC2 instances if load increases, but it requires human intervention, just like it did on-premises. You've gained the operational benefits of running on AWS — no more hardware to maintain, better disaster recovery options — but you haven't achieved elasticity. The application scales the way it always did, which is to say, poorly and expensively.

Now contrast this with a Replatform or Refactor strategy where you've redesigned the application to be stateless. User sessions are stored in Amazon ElastiCache or DynamoDB, not on local disk. Configuration is externalized to AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store or Secrets Manager. The application tier is fronted by an Application Load Balancer, and the EC2 instances are part of an Auto Scaling Group configured with target tracking policies. As traffic increases, the Auto Scaling Group automatically launches additional instances; as traffic drops, it terminates them. No human intervention required. The application now scales horizontally and elastically, and your costs align with demand. This is the difference that architectural investment makes.

The database tier presents its own scaling challenges. A traditional relational database like Oracle or SQL Server running on a single large EC2 instance (a Rehost pattern) scales vertically, which means stopping the database, resizing the instance, and restarting it — the same downtime-inducing process you'd have on-premises. If you Replatform that database to Amazon RDS, you gain operational benefits (automated backups, patching, Multi-AZ failover), but the scaling model is still primarily vertical. To achieve true horizontal read scalability, you need to implement read replicas, offloading query traffic from the primary database — a pattern we explored in section 3.1.3.3. For even greater scalability and elasticity, a Refactor strategy might involve migrating to Amazon Aurora, which supports up to 15 low-latency read replicas and can automatically add or remove replicas based on demand using Aurora Auto Scaling. Or, for the right workload, you might choose Amazon DynamoDB, which scales horizontally by design and offers both provisioned and on-demand capacity modes.

The point is this: scalability in the cloud isn't just a function of AWS's service capabilities. It's a function of how you design your application to leverage those capabilities. The migration strategy you select determines how much architectural work you're committing to, which in turn determines how scalable your application will be once it lands in AWS.

#### Enabling Horizontal Scaling Through Stateless Design

We covered the principles of stateless application design extensively in section 3.1.3.1, including the various strategies for achieving statelessness (external session stores, client-side state, token-based authentication) and the trade-offs involved. It's worth reiterating here that statelessness is the foundational architectural pattern that enables elastic, horizontal scaling in a migrated application. Without it, you cannot safely add or remove instances behind a load balancer, because you cannot guarantee that a user's second request will land on the same server that handled their first request.

For applications being migrated from on-premises environments where stickiness (session affinity) was the norm — "pin each user to a specific server for the duration of their session" — this is a significant architectural shift. It requires refactoring the application to externalize state, typically by using a service like Amazon ElastiCache (Redis or Memcached) to store session data or by adopting token-based authentication using Amazon Cognito and JSON Web Tokens (JWTs), as we discussed in section 3.1.4.3. These aren't trivial changes, but they're the changes that unlock cloud-native scalability.

If you're unable or unwilling to make these changes — perhaps because the application is a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) product where you don't control the source code, or because the refactoring effort is prohibitively expensive — you can still run the application on AWS, but you'll need to accept the limitations. You might use an Application Load Balancer with sticky sessions enabled, but you'll lose some of the fault tolerance and scalability benefits that come with a fully stateless design, as we detailed in section 3.1.3.1. The application will scale, but not as efficiently or automatically as a cloud-native architecture would.

#### Applying Cloud-Native Scaling Patterns to Migrated Workloads

Once you've achieved statelessness, the actual implementation of auto-scaling follows the patterns we've explored throughout this textbook. You configure an Auto Scaling Group with launch templates that define the instance configuration (AMI, instance type, security groups, IAM role). You attach the Auto Scaling Group to an Application Load Balancer or Network Load Balancer. You define scaling policies — target tracking (e.g., "maintain average CPU utilization at 50%"), step scaling (e.g., "add two instances if CPU exceeds 80%"), or scheduled scaling (e.g., "scale up every morning at 8 AM before the business day starts"). The Auto Scaling Group monitors metrics via Amazon CloudWatch and takes action accordingly.

For containerized applications — an increasingly common migration target for modernization efforts — the scaling mechanisms are similar in principle but implemented through container orchestration platforms. Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS both offer service-level auto-scaling that adjusts the number of running container tasks based on metrics like CPU, memory, or custom CloudWatch metrics. We discussed these services in the context of public-facing applications in section 3.1.3.3. For migrated applications, the key insight is that containerization itself can be a Replatform strategy that enables better scalability even if you haven't fully refactored the application. By packaging a legacy application into a container, you gain the operational benefits of orchestration (automated deployment, health checks, rolling updates) and the ability to scale horizontally by running multiple container replicas, even if the application wasn't originally designed for that pattern.

::: {.callout-box data-type="sidebar"}

### The Serverless Migration Path: Eliminating Scaling Concerns Entirely

There's another architectural pattern that represents the ultimate expression of cloud-native scalability: serverless computing. When you Refactor an application to use AWS Lambda and other serverless services like Amazon API Gateway, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon S3, you're not just achieving automatic scaling — you're eliminating the concept of "servers to scale" entirely. The cloud provider handles all capacity management transparently, and you pay only for the actual compute time consumed, measured in milliseconds.

This pattern is particularly powerful for certain types of migrated workloads. Consider a traditional batch processing application that runs nightly reports on-premises. In the old model, you needed a dedicated server (or cluster of servers) powerful enough to handle the peak load during the batch window, but that server sat idle for the other 22 hours of the day. A Rehost migration would simply move that server to an EC2 instance — same problem, different location. But if you Refactor the batch job to run as a Lambda function triggered by an Amazon EventBridge schedule, the compute capacity appears exactly when needed, processes the workload across as many concurrent Lambda invocations as required (up to your account's concurrency limit), and then disappears. No servers to manage, no capacity to pre-provision, and costs that scale linearly with the actual work performed.

Similarly, internal APIs that were once hosted on application servers can be migrated to a serverless architecture using Amazon API Gateway fronting AWS Lambda functions. As we detailed in section 3.1.3.3, this pattern provides automatic, virtually unlimited horizontal scaling. When request volume is low — perhaps during nights and weekends for an internal HR system — you're running zero instances and paying nothing. When request volume spikes — maybe during the annual open enrollment period when all employees are accessing the system — Lambda automatically scales out to handle thousands of concurrent requests. The scaling is instantaneous, limited only by your account's concurrency quotas, not by how fast you can launch EC2 instances.

There's an important caveat: not every workload is a good fit for the serverless model, especially when migrating from traditional architectures. Lambda functions have a maximum execution duration of 15 minutes, which rules out long-running batch jobs or processes that need to maintain state across extended periods. They also have memory limits (up to 10 GB as of this writing) and deployment package size constraints, which can be challenging for applications with large dependencies. And perhaps most critically, Lambda functions experience "cold starts" — the latency incurred when a function is invoked after being idle, as AWS provisions the execution environment. For latency-sensitive internal applications, this can be problematic, though you can mitigate it using Provisioned Concurrency, which we discussed in section 3.1.3.3.

The architectural decision framework for serverless migration is straightforward: if your workload can be decomposed into stateless, short-lived, event-driven functions, and if you can tolerate (or mitigate) cold start latency, then serverless is often the most scalable and cost-effective option. If your workload involves long-running processes, requires persistent connections, or has complex state management needs that don't map cleanly to external state stores, then containers or traditional EC2-based architectures remain the better choice. Many successful migrations end up with a hybrid model: some components refactored to serverless functions, others modernized as containers, and perhaps some legacy components remaining on EC2 instances, all interconnected via API Gateway, load balancers, and message queues.

:::

Regardless of whether you're using EC2 Auto Scaling Groups, container orchestration, or serverless functions, implementing automatic scaling is only half the battle. The other half is ensuring you have the observability and operational discipline to tune your scaling policies over time. A poorly configured Auto Scaling Group — one that scales too aggressively, wasting money on unused capacity, or too conservatively, causing performance degradation — is arguably worse than not scaling at all, because it creates a false sense of security.

This is where Amazon CloudWatch becomes critical. You need to establish comprehensive monitoring of your scaling metrics: not just the metrics that trigger scaling actions (like CPU utilization or request count), but also the business-level metrics that indicate whether your scaling is actually effective. Are response times staying within acceptable bounds during scale-up events? Are error rates spiking during scale-down events because you're terminating instances too aggressively? Is your application reaching its scaling targets fast enough to handle unexpected traffic bursts, or are you consistently under-provisioned for the first few minutes of a spike?

For more complex, distributed applications, particularly those following microservices patterns after a Refactor migration, AWS X-Ray provides the distributed tracing capabilities necessary to understand how scaling in one component affects the performance of downstream components. If your front-end API tier scales beautifully but your backend database doesn't, your users will still experience slow response times, and the root cause may not be immediately obvious from simple CloudWatch metrics alone.

The lesson here is that achieving cloud-native scalability for migrated applications is a spectrum, not a binary state. On one end, you have a pure Rehost with minimal changes and minimal scalability gains. On the other end, you have a complete Refactor to a microservices architecture with containers, serverless functions, and managed databases, offering maximum elasticity and cost efficiency. Most real-world migrations fall somewhere in between, with architects making pragmatic trade-offs based on timelines, budgets, and business priorities. The key is to make those trade-offs consciously, understanding how each choice affects the scalability characteristics of the resulting architecture, and to invest in the observability and operational practices necessary to optimize that architecture over time.

### Database Scaling Strategies for Hybrid and Migrating Workloads

The database tier presents unique scaling challenges in a migration context, because databases are often the most stateful, performance-sensitive, and business-critical components of an application stack. Unlike web servers or application servers, which can often be scaled horizontally by simply adding more identical instances behind a load balancer, databases require careful architectural consideration. They hold the authoritative copy of your data, they must maintain consistency guarantees, and their performance characteristics directly impact every layer of the application above them. When that database needs to operate across two environments — on-premises and AWS — during a migration, or when it needs to serve hybrid application workloads indefinitely, the scaling strategies become even more complex.

The core challenge is this: traditional relational databases were designed to scale vertically within a single data center, not horizontally across geographically distributed locations. When you're running a database on-premises and want to scale it, you typically upgrade to a larger server with more CPU cores, more RAM, and faster disks. This vertical scaling approach has hard limits and creates potential single points of failure. Cloud databases like Amazon RDS and Amazon Aurora offer better vertical scaling options (you can resize instances more easily) and horizontal read scaling through read replicas, but these patterns assume your entire database infrastructure is in the cloud. During a migration, or in a sustained hybrid architecture, you need strategies that work across both environments while maintaining acceptable performance, consistency, and operational complexity.

This section explores three distinct scenarios. First, we'll examine how to use AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) with Change Data Capture (CDC) to create a hybrid database scaling pattern during migration, where the primary database remains on-premises but read-heavy workloads are offloaded to AWS. Second, we'll discuss the architectural considerations and trade-offs of this approach — replication lag, cost implications, and the eventual cutover strategy. Finally, we'll contrast post-migration database scaling options available entirely within AWS, cross-referencing the detailed patterns we explored in section 3.1.3.3 but focusing specifically on how migration strategy impacts your ultimate scaling capabilities.

#### Hybrid Read Scaling with DMS and Change Data Capture

One of the most powerful patterns for scaling databases during a migration is to use **AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)** to continuously replicate data from your on-premises primary database to a read replica in AWS. This isn't just a migration technique — it's a hybrid scaling architecture. By keeping your primary, write-master database on-premises while creating synchronized read replicas in the cloud, you can offload read-intensive workloads to AWS, effectively scaling your database tier horizontally across environments.

The mechanism that makes this possible is **Change Data Capture (CDC)**. CDC is a technique for tracking changes to database records in real time by monitoring the database's transaction log. When you configure DMS with CDC enabled, it doesn't just perform a one-time bulk copy of your data. Instead, it continuously reads the transaction log of your source database (whether that's Oracle, SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL, or another supported engine), captures every insert, update, and delete operation, and applies those changes to the target database in AWS. The result is a near-real-time replica that stays synchronized with the on-premises primary as long as the DMS replication task is running.

From a scaling perspective, this is transformative. Imagine you have an on-premises Oracle database that's struggling under the combined load of transactional writes (orders being placed, inventory being updated) and heavy analytical reads (business intelligence reports, dashboard queries). The traditional solution would be to upgrade to a larger on-premises server, but you're already running on the biggest hardware you can procure, and adding more on-premises capacity is expensive and time-consuming. Instead, you configure DMS to replicate this Oracle database to Amazon RDS for Oracle (or, if you're willing to do some application refactoring, to a PostgreSQL-compatible target using DMS's heterogeneous migration capabilities). Now you can redirect all of your read-heavy reporting workloads to query the RDS instance in AWS, while writes continue to hit the on-premises primary. You've effectively doubled your database's read capacity without buying new hardware or taking downtime.

Let's be precise about the architecture. You deploy a **DMS replication instance** — an EC2 instance that DMS manages on your behalf — in a VPC that has network connectivity to your on-premises database (typically via VPN or Direct Connect). You configure a **source endpoint** pointing to your on-premises database, providing the connection string, credentials, and any TLS settings required. You configure a **target endpoint** pointing to your RDS instance in AWS. Then you create a **DMS task** that specifies what data to replicate (all tables, a subset, specific schemas) and crucially, you enable **CDC** in the task settings. DMS performs an initial **full load** to copy all existing data, and then it switches into CDC mode, continuously tailing the source database's transaction log and streaming changes to the target.

From the application's perspective, you now have two database endpoints: the on-premises primary for all write operations, and the RDS replica in AWS for read operations. This requires application-level awareness — your code needs to route queries appropriately. For many applications, this is a straightforward change: update your reporting tools, BI systems, or analytics dashboards to point at the AWS endpoint, while leaving your transactional application code pointed at the on-premises primary. In some cases, you might use a read/write splitting proxy or modify your ORM configuration to handle this routing automatically. The key point is that this hybrid read scaling pattern works even while the primary database remains firmly planted on-premises, which is exactly the situation you're in during the middle of a migration project.

#### Architectural Trade-Offs: Replication Lag, Cost, and Cutover Planning

This hybrid database scaling pattern is powerful, but it's not without trade-offs. The most critical consideration is **replication lag** — the time delay between when a change is committed on the on-premises primary and when that change appears in the AWS replica. For a CDC-based replication system like DMS, lag is influenced by several factors: the volume of change traffic (how many writes per second), the network bandwidth and latency between on-premises and AWS, the processing power of the DMS replication instance, and the write capacity of the target database.

In a typical well-configured DMS setup with adequate bandwidth and appropriately sized instances, replication lag is measured in seconds — often single-digit seconds for moderate workloads. For many read-heavy use cases, this is perfectly acceptable. A business intelligence dashboard that shows yesterday's sales figures doesn't need to reflect data written three seconds ago; a lag of 5-10 seconds is imperceptible. However, for workloads that require strong read-after-write consistency — where a user updates a record and immediately queries for that update — this lag can be problematic. If your application writes to the on-premises primary and then immediately reads from the AWS replica, it might not see its own write, leading to confusing behavior or data inconsistency errors.

The solution is to carefully categorize your read workloads by their consistency requirements. Queries that can tolerate eventual consistency — reports, analytics, historical data lookups — are ideal candidates for routing to the AWS replica. Queries that require strong consistency — "show me the order I just placed", "what's my current account balance" — must continue hitting the on-premises primary. This is an architectural pattern you'll need to implement in your application logic or through a smart routing layer. It's the same challenge that arises with any read replica strategy, whether fully on-premises or fully in AWS, but it's worth calling out explicitly in the hybrid context because the network hop to AWS can increase lag compared to a local replica.

From a **cost perspective**, running this hybrid architecture means paying for dual database infrastructure. You're maintaining your on-premises server (with all its associated hardware, power, and data center costs) *and* you're paying for an RDS instance in AWS (charged per hour based on instance type) *and* you're paying for the DMS replication instance that sits between them *and* you're potentially paying for data transfer charges if you're sending hundreds of gigabytes of change data over a VPN or Direct Connect connection. This is a temporary, transitional state, not a long-term cost-optimized architecture. The business case for this pattern is that it enables you to offload read traffic immediately — potentially deferring an expensive on-premises hardware upgrade — while you prepare for the eventual full migration to AWS.

This brings us to the **cutover strategy**. The hybrid read scaling pattern is typically a stepping stone, not a destination. At some point, you'll want to complete the migration by promoting the AWS replica to become the new primary and decommissioning the on-premises database entirely. DMS supports this with a relatively straightforward cutover process: you stop writes to the on-premises database (put the application in maintenance mode), allow DMS to catch up fully (lag goes to zero), verify that the AWS database contains all expected data, and then reconfigure your application to point all reads *and* writes at the AWS database. The on-premises database can then be powered down. This is a planned downtime event, but with proper preparation, the downtime window can be measured in minutes, not hours.

The trade-off between maintaining a hybrid architecture long-term versus completing the migration is a business decision. Some organizations operate hybrid databases indefinitely because of regulatory data residency requirements, or because certain on-premises applications cannot easily be refactored to accommodate the network latency of reaching a cloud database. For these scenarios, the hybrid read scaling pattern becomes a sustained operational model. But for most migrations, the goal is to reach a fully cloud-based database architecture as quickly as is practical, unlocking the full scaling, availability, and cost optimization capabilities that AWS-native database services provide.

#### Post-Migration Database Scaling in AWS

Once your database has been fully migrated to AWS — whether through the DMS-assisted cutover process described above or through other migration strategies — you gain access to a much richer set of scaling options than were available in the hybrid state. We covered these patterns extensively in section 3.1.3.3, so we won't repeat all the technical details here, but it's worth revisiting them specifically in the migration context to understand how your migration strategy impacts your ultimate scalability.

If you performed a **Rehost migration**, moving your on-premises database to a self-managed database on an EC2 instance, your scaling options remain largely unchanged from what they were on-premises. You can scale vertically by stopping the instance and resizing it to a larger instance type (easier than swapping physical hardware, but still requires downtime). You can implement read replicas manually using native database replication features (e.g., Oracle Data Guard, SQL Server Always On, MySQL replication), but you're responsible for configuring, monitoring, and failing over these replicas yourself. You've gained the operational flexibility of the cloud — no hardware procurement, no data center capacity planning — but you haven't fundamentally changed the database's scalability architecture.

If you performed a **Replatform migration** to a managed database service like **Amazon RDS**, you've taken a significant step forward. RDS handles operational toil like automated backups, patching, and monitoring, but more importantly for scalability, it provides straightforward mechanisms for vertical scaling (resize the instance class with minimal downtime using RDS's maintenance window) and horizontal read scaling through **RDS Read Replicas**. You can create up to five read replicas per primary instance, each of which can serve read-only queries, and you can even create replicas in different AWS Regions for low-latency access by globally distributed users or for disaster recovery purposes. RDS automates the replication setup and management, making it operationally far simpler than self-managed replication on EC2.

For even greater scalability, a **Replatform to Amazon Aurora** (whether Aurora MySQL or Aurora PostgreSQL) offers significant advantages. Aurora supports up to 15 low-latency read replicas that share the same underlying storage cluster, meaning writes are automatically visible across all replicas with minimal lag. Aurora also offers **Aurora Auto Scaling**, which can automatically add or remove read replicas based on CPU utilization or connection count, providing elastic read capacity without manual intervention. And if your workload is intermittent or unpredictable, **Aurora Serverless** (v1 for MySQL 5.6/5.7 and PostgreSQL, v2 for newer versions) can automatically scale the database's compute capacity up or down in response to actual load, even scaling to zero during idle periods to minimize costs. These are capabilities that simply don't exist in a traditional on-premises database or even in a basic RDS deployment.

::: {.callout-box data-type="sidebar"}

### Why Choose RDS Over Aurora?

While the text highlights Aurora's superior scalability, the choice of a database involves crucial trade-offs. An organization might choose Amazon RDS for several key reasons:

* **Cost & Predictability:** With RDS, You provision a specific amount of EBS storage and you pay a fixed monthly price for that storage, regardless of how much you use it. You also pay for provisioned IOPS if you use `io1` or `io2` volumes. This is a very **predictable** billing model. In contrast, you don't provision storage for Aurora; instead, the storage grows automatically as you add data, and you're charged for the storage you actually use and for every I/O operation. For I/O-intensive applications (constantly reading and writing many small blocks of data), the fixed cost of RDS with Provisioned IOPS can be significantly cheaper and more predictable than Aurora's variable I/O charges. **RDS** is like renting a car with a fixed daily rate and unlimited mileage, while **Aurora** is like a ride-sharing service where you pay per mile. Ride-sharing is cheaper for short, infrequent trips, but costs can add up quickly on a long road trip.
* **Engine Compatibility:** While Aurora is "wire-compatible" with MySQL and PostgreSQL, it is not the *exact* same engine. It's a custom-built, cloud-native engine that speaks the same protocol. RDS offers the native MySQL and PostgreSQL engines, ensuring 100% compatibility. This is critical for applications that rely on specific engine behaviors, versions, or extensions that may not be available or may behave differently on the Aurora-compatible editions. This minimizes migration risks. 
* **Simplicity & Free Tier:** For smaller workloads, development environments, or applications that are not performance-critical, Aurora's advanced architecture can be overkill. RDS provides a simpler, more straightforward solution. Importantly, **RDS has a generous Free Tier**, while Aurora does not, making it the default choice for experimentation, learning, and small-scale projects.

| Feature | Amazon RDS | Amazon Aurora |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Best For** | Stable, predictable, or I/O-heavy workloads. Maximum engine compatibility. | High-performance, highly-available, and variable workloads needing elastic scale. |
| **Cost Model** | **Predictable:** Pay for provisioned instance hours and storage (EBS). | **Variable:** Pay for instance hours, actual storage used, and **per I/O operation**. |
| **Performance** | Good to excellent, dependent on EBS volume type. | Highest performance, with a custom storage backend. |
| **Availability** | High (Multi-AZ with synchronous replication). | Highest (Data replicated 6 ways across 3 AZs). |
| **Read Replicas** | Up to 5 (MySQL/Postgres) with potential for replication lag. | Up to 15 with very low replication lag. |
| **Free Tier** | **Yes** ✅ | **No** ❌ |

For the SAA-C03 exam, the key is to read the scenario carefully. If the question mentions a need for the **highest possible performance and availability** or **elastic scaling**, think **Aurora**. If it mentions a **cost-sensitive**, **predictable**, or **I/O-heavy workload**, or a need for a specific engine feature, **RDS** is likely the better choice.

:::

If you performed a **Refactor migration** to a cloud-native NoSQL database like **Amazon DynamoDB**, you've moved to a fundamentally different scaling model. DynamoDB is designed to scale horizontally across dozens or hundreds of partitions, handling millions of requests per second if needed. It offers both **provisioned capacity** mode (where you specify read and write capacity units and can manually or automatically scale them) and **on-demand capacity** mode (where DynamoDB automatically scales to handle whatever load you throw at it, charging per-request). For read-heavy workloads, DynamoDB supports **Global Tables** for multi-region replication and **DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)** for microsecond-latency in-memory caching. The scalability ceiling is orders of magnitude higher than a traditional relational database, but you've paid for this with the need to redesign your data model and potentially refactor application code to work with DynamoDB's key-value and document-oriented API.

The lesson here is that your migration strategy has a direct and lasting impact on how your database scales post-migration. A Rehost gives you operational flexibility but limited scalability improvements. A Replatform to managed services like RDS or Aurora unlocks cloud-native scaling features with minimal application changes. A Refactor to services like DynamoDB provides ultimate scalability but requires the most significant upfront investment in redesign. The choice depends on your application's requirements, your timeline, and your team's capabilities. There's no one-size-fits-all answer, but understanding the full spectrum of options — and how each relates to the hybrid scaling patterns you might use during migration — is essential for making informed architectural decisions.

The key architectural insight is that database scaling during migration is a distinct problem from database scaling after migration. During migration, you're operating in a constrained, hybrid state where you must work within the limitations of having data in two places. Patterns like DMS with CDC for hybrid read scaling are powerful tools for this phase, allowing you to offload work to AWS even before you've fully committed to the migration. After migration, you can leverage the full power of AWS-native database services, but the scalability characteristics of your post-migration database are largely determined by the migration strategy you chose. Understanding this progression — from hybrid to cloud-native, from constrained to elastic — is fundamental to designing successful migration architectures.

### Scaling Hybrid Container Workloads

Containers have become the de facto standard for packaging and deploying modern applications, and for good reason. They provide consistency across environments, enable efficient resource utilization, and simplify the operational model for managing complex, distributed systems. But what happens when your containers need to run not just in AWS, but also on-premises? Perhaps you have data sovereignty requirements that mandate certain processing stays within your own data center. Perhaps you're running latency-sensitive applications on factory floors or retail stores where every millisecond of network round-trip time matters. Or perhaps you've made significant capital investments in on-premises infrastructure that still has years of useful life, and you want to leverage that capacity while gradually shifting workloads to the cloud. These are the scenarios where hybrid container architectures become essential.

The challenge of scaling containerized applications across on-premises and cloud environments is fundamentally different from scaling purely cloud-native container workloads. In a cloud-only architecture, you can rely on services like Amazon ECS or Amazon EKS to handle orchestration, scaling, health monitoring, and networking, all managed by AWS. But when you extend containers to on-premises infrastructure, you face a new set of questions: Who manages the orchestration control plane? How do you maintain consistent operational practices across both environments? How do you scale capacity in your data center when you don't have AWS's virtually unlimited pool of resources? And perhaps most critically, how do you avoid creating two entirely separate operational silos that double your complexity and cognitive load?

AWS offers two primary services for hybrid container workloads — **Amazon ECS Anywhere** and **Amazon EKS Anywhere** — and understanding the difference between them is critical for the exam and for real-world architecture decisions. These aren't interchangeable solutions; they represent fundamentally different operational philosophies and technical architectures. ECS Anywhere extends AWS's fully managed ECS control plane to on-premises servers, allowing you to manage containers running in your data center using the same service that manages containers in AWS, with AWS operating the orchestrator. EKS Anywhere, by contrast, provides you with the tools to deploy and manage a complete, customer-operated Kubernetes cluster on-premises, with optional connectivity back to AWS for visibility and management. The first is "AWS manages everything, everywhere." The second is "you manage your own cluster, with AWS's help."
